morningLine: A mouse, tiled windows, and a $99 invitation to try another way of working.

lead.headline: Windows finally ships for the IBM PC
lead.dek: Microsoft’s $99 graphical environment arrives November 20 after a long wait.
body: Microsoft has shipped Windows, giving owners of DOS personal computers a new way to move among programs with menus, icons and a mouse. The November 20 retail arrival ends the wait that followed its original 1983 announcement. The first US retail revision is 1.01, part of the Windows 1.0 product family.

The $99 introductory software price buys an operating environment above MS-DOS, not a replacement computer or a complete system. DOS, suitable graphics hardware and a mouse remain separate considerations. Published requirements call for at least 256K of memory, two double-sided floppy drives and a graphics adapter; 512K and a hard disk are recommended for running multiple programs or using DOS 3.0 and higher.

Windows tiles its application windows rather than offering the overlapping desktop familiar to some other graphical systems. Scroll bars, dialog boxes and menus bring a visual vocabulary to machines more often addressed through typed commands. Paint, Notepad, Calculator, Calendar, Card File and a clock provide practical starting points.

There is room for play, too: Reversi comes in the package. For the PC owner, this week’s immediate question is what that visual environment can do on the hardware already on the desk. Shipment is the milestone; the platform’s eventual reach is not yet a result to report.

stories.headline: Kampfgruppe takes the gaming crown
body: Computer Gaming World’s November/December awards put SSI’s Kampfgruppe at the top of the ballot. The tactical World War II simulation wins both the overall Game of the Year honor and the wargame category. These are period magazine awards for existing games, not a claim of a new release this week.

The magazine points to scenario generation and computer-managed battlefield bookkeeping as strengths. Line-of-sight and opportunity-fire calculations that can slow a tabletop battle become part of the machine’s work. It reports 8,000 copies sold and an SSI expectation of 25,000 eventually; the latter remains a forecast.

Ultima III wins Adventure, Seven Cities of Gold wins Strategy, and F-15 Strike Eagle wins Action. The feature reports sales above 100,000 for Seven Cities and 100,000 for F-15, figures attributed to the period report rather than an independently audited tally.

stories.headline: Amiga puts color under the programmer’s control
body: Charles Brannon’s November COMPUTE! feature examines the Amiga’s custom graphics machinery. A 4,096-color universe and animation support give programmers a lively new canvas, alongside a 68000 processor, stereo sound and multitasking.

The palette needs careful reading: ordinary modes use 16 or 32 selected colors depending on mode, not all 4,096 at once in every display. The article also describes a 640-by-400 high-resolution bitmap mode and the built-in 880K disk drive. This is current-month technical coverage of an already introduced computer, not a new launch during this week.

stories.headline: Fastlink puts a premium price on speed
body: Arlan R. Levitan’s November COMPUTE! telecomputing column describes DCA’s Fastlink reaching roughly 10,000 bits per second on local voice-grade lines. The reported figures fall to about 8,000 on the leading long-distance carrier and about 7,000 on other common carriers. Those are the column’s claims, not independent benchmarks.

The internal PC-compatible version lists at $1,995 with special Crosstalk software; an external RS-232 model is $2,395. Both ends need Fastlinks for the high-speed connection. Other modems meet it at 300 or 1200 bps, while an equal two-way load divides the claimed maximum to about 5,000 bps in each direction.

briefs.headline: Online services add more than conversation
briefs.summary: COMPUTE! November online-service roundup describes Delphi’s AP news and computer-owner SIGs, and Dow Jones college and medical databases. Features were reported this month, not necessarily launched this week.

briefs.headline: Apple and Microsoft sign a display agreement
briefs.summary: On November 22 the companies enter a visual-display licensing agreement. Retrospective court records establish the date and terms; this archive note does not imply ordinary readers had the private contract that week. It was not a blanket license to every future Macintosh feature.

market.headline: The price of a new interface
market.summary: Windows starts at $99 for software, but DOS and suitable hardware remain separate. At the communications counter, Fastlink asks $1,995 for its internal version and a matching high-speed peer at the far end. The sticker price is only the beginning of a workable system.

worldAnchor.headline: Reagan and Gorbachev meet in Geneva
worldAnchor.summary: First meeting between the two leaders, November 19–21; November 21 joint statement calls for accelerated arms negotiations and further meetings. No arms-control treaty was signed at this summit.

bbsNote.headline: Faster links, richer services, and a very real hourly bill
bbsNote.summary: Verified November COMPUTE! coverage, principally printed pages 28–29 and 133. Posts below are editorial summaries, not recovered BBS messages or invented user quotations.

posts.platform: DCA Fastlink / IBM PC and RS-232
posts.text: The $1,995 internal and $2,395 external models promise about 10,000 bps on local lines; high-speed peers must both be Fastlinks. Current-month technical coverage, not this week’s launch.
November roundup says 2400-bps service has been available since June at an extra $5 an hour; AP news, sports and financial information and Commodore, Apple II, Macintosh and Atari SIGs are described.

Roundup describes a planned October 1 start in most covered US areas, with exclusions in four New England states. Starter kit $9.95 with first hour; subsequent off-peak access 9 cents/minute and weekday daytime 22 cents/minute, no monthly minimum or extra 1200-bps fee. Plans and advertised terms are not independent confirmation of actual nationwide operation.

curiosity.headline: A $599 box promises to turn a Commodore 64 into an Apple II Plus
curiosity.summary: Mimic Systems’ Spartan advertisement in November COMPUTE! offers a surprisingly literal route across the home-computer divide.
curiosity.detail: The ad prices Spartan at US $599 and claims Apple II Plus hardware/software capabilities, 64K RAM expansion, four software-selectable Commodore cartridge slots and an 8-bit parallel port. These are advertiser claims, not the magazine’s tested findings. Do not silently call it a software emulator download.
